Illinois property tax FAQ

When are Illinois board of review complaints due?

Complaints are generally due within 30 days after publication of the assessment list (35 ILCS 200/16-55). Confirm the date with your county.

How is a home assessed for property tax in Illinois?

Under 35 ILCS 200/9-145, property in most Illinois counties is valued at 33 1/3% of its fair cash value. The exception is a county with more than 200,000 residents that classifies property, and Cook County is one: its Assessor's page shows an assessment level of 10% for residential property in its sample calculation. A state equalizer is then applied to produce the equalized assessed value (EAV).

Your bill depends on two things at once: the assessment of your property and the money your local taxing districts need to run during the year. The Property Tax Appeal Board says assessments are set by county assessing officials, which means the Cook County Assessor in Cook and a township assessor or supervisor of assessments in the other counties.

When must I file an appeal of my Illinois assessment?

A complaint to the board of review must be filed within 30 calendar days after the assessment list is published (35 ILCS 200/16-55(d)). In counties under 3,000,000 residents the chief county assessment officer publishes the list in a newspaper, with the notice carrying the appeal deadline, and the statute sets a December 31 publication cutoff. The notice tells taxpayers to talk to the township assessor first, then appeal to the board if not satisfied.

Mailed complaints count as filed on the postmark date, and complaints must be in writing. Where a change of $100,000 or more in assessed value is sought, the board serves a copy on the affected taxing districts at least 14 days before the hearing. Cook County runs its own calendar by township, so ask the Assessor or the Board of Review for your township's dates.

  • Start with the assessor if your county or township has one.
  • Put the complaint in writing and send it inside the 30-day window.
  • Keep comparable sales, an appraisal or a recent purchase contract as evidence.

What can the Property Tax Appeal Board do after the board of review rules?

The next step is the Property Tax Appeal Board (PTAB), a five-member body appointed by the Governor. A petition is due 30 days after the board of review's written decision, and PTAB warns that an appeal is rejected if it is late. Residential appeals seeking a change under $100,000 in assessed value can rely on comparable properties or an appraisal.

PTAB has limits. It decides the correct assessment of a property on equity and the weight of the evidence. It has no jurisdiction over the amount of a tax bill or the tax rate used to compute it, and it cannot exempt property from tax. A separate petition is needed for each assessment year, and PTAB accepts e-filed appeals, while faxed or emailed appeals are not accepted.

How and when are Illinois property tax bills issued?

Illinois bills in installments. In a county of 3,000,000 or more residents, estimated first-installment bills go out by January 31 at 55% of the prior year's total bill, and actual bills with the balance follow by June 30 under 35 ILCS 200/21-30. The county board may adopt four installments by ordinance, and counties with fewer residents may adopt an accelerated billing method.

In Cook County, the Assessor reports that second-installment bills for tax year 2025 were mailed on September 1, 2026 and were due October 1, 2026. Ask the treasurer or collector's office for the due dates that apply to your parcel, since schedules vary by county.

Which exemptions and relief programs can lower an Illinois bill?

The Property Tax Code has general, senior, disability, veterans and home improvement exemptions. They are explained on our Illinois homestead exemption page. The Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral Program under 320 ILCS 30 works differently: the county collector defers part or all of a bill and records a lien.

To qualify a taxpayer must be 65 by June 1 of the deferral year, have owned and lived in the property for at least three years, and have household income no higher than the statutory cap, which is $75,000 for tax year 2025, $77,000 for 2026 and $79,000 for 2027 and after. Applications reach the collector's office by March 1. From tax year 2022 the deferral is capped at $7,500 per taxpayer per year, and the total with interest may not exceed 80% of the taxpayer's equity. Interest runs at 3% a year for tax year 2023 and later.

The lien is a first lien. The statute says no sale or transfer may be closed and recorded until the deferred taxes and interest are paid, unless the collector certifies in writing that a prompt payment arrangement exists. Repayment comes due one year after the taxpayer's death or 90 days after the home stops qualifying.

What happens if Illinois property taxes go unpaid?

Unpaid taxes can lead to a tax sale. Property sold at a tax sale may be redeemed before three years pass from the date of sale, with shorter periods for some property types such as vacant parcels, so ask the county clerk which period applies to a parcel. The deed stage requires notice, and a tax deed petition can be filed in the last six months of the redemption period.

If taxes stay unsold, the collector can apply for a scavenger sale. The minimum bid is $250, or one-half of the tax if the total liability is under $500, and the sale is not final until the court confirms it. Confirmation wipes out the in rem lien of the general taxes, but it does not remove the owner's personal liability for them.

  • Redemption from a scavenger sale carries interest in set steps, such as 12% when redeemed between two and six months after the sale and 24% between six and twelve months.
  • Pay the redemption amount to the county collector, not to the buyer.
  • Get a written payoff figure from the title company ahead of scheduling the closing.

What taxes apply when I sell an Illinois house?

The state transfer tax is collected by the county recorder of deeds or registrar of titles through revenue stamps, now electronic, at a rate of 50¢ per $500 (35 ILCS 200/31-15). A county can layer its own levy on top, and home rule municipalities may impose another. Buyer and seller complete Form PTAX-203, which can be filed through MyDec at MyTax Illinois in participating counties.

Property taxes for the sale year are normally prorated between buyer and seller at closing, and Illinois bills the prior year in arrears. Request the proration method the title company will use and which installment is still open. A seller who knows of a senior deferral lien, a delinquent bill or a pending appeal should tell the buyer and title company at the start.

When is an Illinois assessment complaint due?

Thirty calendar days after the assessment list is published is the cutoff at the county board of review. A mailed complaint counts as filed on its postmark date (35 ILCS 200/16-55).

Can PTAB change the rate on my tax bill?

No. PTAB can decide the correct assessment, but it has no jurisdiction over the tax bill amount, the tax rate or the exempt status of property.

What is the cutoff for a PTAB petition?

The petition goes in 30 days after the board of review's written decision, or after written notice of final township multipliers. Late petitions are rejected.

Can I defer Illinois property taxes as a senior?

Yes, under 320 ILCS 30 if you are 65 by June 1, have owned and lived in the home three years and meet the income cap. Apply to the county collector by March 1.

Do unpaid property taxes have to be paid at closing?

Deferred taxes and interest must be paid, or a payment arrangement certified in writing by the collector, before a sale of deferred property can be closed and recorded. For delinquent bills, ask the title company for a payoff figure.

Illinois homestead exemption FAQ

Where do I apply for a homestead exemption?

With the county chief county assessment officer. Dates and forms are set locally.

What homestead exemptions can an Illinois homeowner claim?

Illinois lets owners who live in their house claim several exemptions that shrink the value the tax rate is applied to: the general homestead exemption, the senior exemption, the low-income senior assessment freeze, the exemption for persons with disabilities, the veterans exemptions and a home improvement exemption. All of them are written into Article 15 of the Property Tax Code, 35 ILCS 200.

Each one cuts the equalized assessed value (EAV), which is the taxed value after the state equalizer is applied. It does not subtract dollars from the bill directly. The saving depends on your EAV reduction multiplied by the local tax rate, and each tax bill carries its own rate.

  • General homestead exemption (Section 15-175), for owner-occupied homes.
  • Senior citizens homestead exemption (15-170), for owners 65 and older.
  • Low-income senior citizens assessment freeze (15-172).
  • Persons with disabilities (15-168) and veterans (15-169).
  • Home improvement exemption (15-180), for added value from improvements.

How much does each Illinois exemption take off a home's value?

The general exemption removes the growth in your EAV above the 1977 level, up to a cap that depends on the county. Since taxable year 2023 the cap is $10,000 in a county of 3,000,000 or more people (Cook), $8,000 in counties touching such a county, and $6,000 in every other county.

The senior exemption is a flat cap on top of that. For taxable years 2023 and later it is $8,000 in Cook and the counties contiguous to it, and $5,000 elsewhere. The table lists the main exemptions with the figures as the statute prints them.

ExemptionWho qualifiesStatutory limit

Veterans with disabilitiesService-connected rating certified by the VA$2,500 (30% to under 50%), $5,000 (50% to under 70%), first $250,000 of EAV at 70% or more

Who qualifies for the senior exemption and the senior freeze?

The senior exemption applies to a home occupied as a residence by a person who is 65 or older, is liable for the real estate taxes and holds title or a recorded legal or equitable interest. A person who turns 65 during the assessment year can apply that same year.

The freeze adds an income test. The household income cap in 35 ILCS 200/15-172 is $65,000 for taxable years 2018 through 2025, $75,000 for 2026, $77,000 for 2027 and $79,000 for 2028 and after. Household income means the combined income of the applicant, a spouse and everyone using the home as a principal residence during the calendar year before the taxable year. The freeze holds the EAV at a base amount, so later assessment growth stops raising the taxed value.

  • An owner enrolled in SNAP, LIHEAP, the Benefit Access program, the Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral Program or AABD may be presumed to meet the income cap.
  • If a qualifying owner dies and the surviving spouse is under 65, the spouse can still receive the freeze for the year before and the year of death.
  • Married people who keep separate residences can claim the freeze for only one of them.
  • An owner who moves to a licensed care facility keeps the exemption while the spouse remains at home or while the house stays unoccupied and owned.

How do veterans and homeowners with disabilities qualify?

The disability exemption is $2,000 off the value. The owner must live in the home, owe the taxes and hold title or a recorded interest. Proof of disability can be Social Security disability eligibility or an Illinois Person with a Disability Identification Card with a Class 2 disability. Anyone else is examined by a physician or other designated provider at their own cost.

Veterans with a service-connected disability get a tiered benefit under Section 15-169, based on the rating the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs certifies as of the application date. A veteran with a rating of 70% or more has the first $250,000 of EAV exempt. From taxable year 2024, a World War II veteran is exempt regardless of the disability level. A surviving spouse who does not remarry keeps the exemption while living in the home, and it can move to a new primary residence if the spouse sells.

A taxpayer cannot combine the disability exemption with the veterans exemption.

Do Illinois homestead exemptions renew on their own?

It depends on the exemption and the county. Outside the large county, the general exemption is applied automatically where the current EAV is higher than the 1977 figure. In Cook County the Assessor's Office renews the Homeowner, Senior, Persons with Disabilities and World War II exemptions each year without a new application, but the Senior Freeze, Returning Veterans and Veterans with Disabilities exemptions must be filed every year.

State law backs part of this: for veterans with disabilities, reapplying is required every year unless the veteran served in World War II or has a permanent and total 100% rating. For persons with disabilities, a county of more than 3,000,000 residents may renew without an annual application for taxable years 2022 through 2027.

  • Review the exemption history on your parcel record each tax year.
  • Late filings are handled as certificates of error in Cook County.

What happens to my exemptions when I sell or move out?

An exemption follows occupancy, not the owner. In a county with 3,000,000 or more residents, if the house is not your principal residence on January 1 of the tax year, you must tell the chief county assessment officer in writing by March 1 of the collection year, or the exemption is treated as erroneous. Notice given on time stops interest and penalties on the wrongly granted exemption for that year.

For a senior who first occupies a home after January 1, the senior exemption is prorated by the days of occupancy divided by 365 (35 ILCS 200/15-170(e)). Sellers should expect the title company to prorate the tax bill at closing and should not count on exemptions staying on the bill after the sale. Ask the county assessor or treasurer for the exemption status of the parcel before you set a price.

A senior who holds a tax deferral under 320 ILCS 30 faces another step. The statute says no sale or transfer can be closed and recorded until the deferred taxes plus accrued interest are paid, unless the collector certifies a payment arrangement in writing.

How can I recover an exemption that was missing from past bills?

In Cook County, a homeowner who should have had an exemption can file a certificate of error. The Assessor's exemptions page lists the years open for recovery as 2025, 2024, 2023, 2022 and 2021, and says the normal filing period has ended for the current cycle, so late applications go through the certificate of error process.

Outside Cook, contact the supervisor of assessments or the county assessor. Ask whether the county uses an application period, which documents it needs, and whether past years can be corrected. Homeowners who inherited a house can claim the senior exemption for the year a parent died if the parent lived there on January 1 and used it as a principal residence, with a death certificate and letters of office or similar paperwork.

More questions about Illinois Homestead Exemption

Is the Illinois general homestead exemption automatic?

In counties with fewer than 3,000,000 residents, yes. The owner receives it automatically when the current EAV exceeds the 1977 EAV, up to the statutory cap (35 ILCS 200/15-175(c)). In Cook County, the Assessor's Office renews the Homeowner Exemption each year once it is applied.

At what age can I claim the Illinois senior exemption?

You can claim it from age 65. A person who will be 65 during the assessment year may apply during that year, using the application period set for the county of residence (35 ILCS 200/15-170(d)).

What is the senior freeze income limit?

The statute sets $65,000 for taxable years 2018 through 2025, $75,000 for 2026, $77,000 for 2027 and $79,000 for 2028 and after. Household income is measured for the calendar year before the taxable year, and the Cook County Assessor lists $65,000 for 2024 income.

Can I get both the disability exemption and the veterans exemption?

No. A taxpayer who claims the veterans exemption under Section 15-169 cannot claim the disability exemption under Section 15-168 for the same property, so the owner chooses one.

Does a homestead exemption affect a cash sale of my house?

It changes the tax bill that is prorated at closing, but it does not block a sale. If you have a senior tax deferral, the deferred taxes and interest must be paid or a payment arrangement certified before closing and recording.

Illinois senior exemption FAQ

What is the senior freeze income limit?

What senior property tax breaks does Illinois offer homeowners?

Illinois has three senior programs that homeowners 65 and older can stack: a flat reduction in assessed value, an assessment freeze for lower income households, and a deferral that postpones the bill itself. The Department of Revenue describes all three in its PIO-74 exemption guide, and the statutes sit in the Property Tax Code and in 320 ILCS 30.

  • Senior Citizens Homestead Exemption, 35 ILCS 200/15-170
  • Low-Income Senior Citizens Assessment Freeze Homestead Exemption, 35 ILCS 200/15-172, often called the senior freeze
  • Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral Program, 320 ILCS 30

The county assessor, called the chief county assessment officer in the statutes, handles the first two. The deferral runs through the county collector.

How much does the Illinois Senior Citizens Homestead Exemption take off?

It cuts equalized assessed value by up to $8,000 in Cook County and in counties contiguous to a county of 3,000,000 or more people, and by up to $5,000 in every other county, for taxable years 2023 and after. Section 15-170 grants it for a home occupied by a person 65 or older who owes the real estate taxes and either is an owner of record or holds a legal or equitable interest shown in a written instrument.

A person who turns 65 during the assessment year can apply that same year. A home first occupied by an eligible person after January 1 gets a pro rata exemption, equal to the county amount divided by 365 and multiplied by the days of qualifying occupancy. In Cook County, the Assessor's office says the senior exemption renews automatically once granted, and that it reduces EAV by $8,000, so the dollar saving depends on the local tax rate shown on the second installment bill.

What is the Illinois senior freeze income limit?

The limit is $75,000 of household income for taxable year 2026, rising to $77,000 for 2027 and $79,000 for 2028 and later, as the Department of Revenue lists in PIO-74 and as 35 ILCS 200/15-172 reads in its current version. Household income is the combined income of the applicant, the spouse and everyone using the home as a principal residence, measured for the calendar year before the taxable year. Veterans' benefits are excluded from "income" under the statute.

Taxable yearIncome limit

Source: 35 ILCS 200/15-172 and Illinois Department of Revenue PIO-74.

What does the senior freeze lock in, and what does it leave alone?

The freeze holds the home's equalized assessed value at a base year level. The base year is the taxable year before the first year the applicant qualifies and applies. If the assessed value later falls below the base, the lower year becomes the new base. The exemption amount each year is the current EAV minus the base amount.

The Department of Revenue points out that the tax bill can still rise when tax rates go up or when improvements added to the home increase its value. The freeze covers the valuation, not the bill. In Cook County, the Assessor says applicants must file every year, and the Assessor's page for the program gives $65,000 or less in the 2024 calendar year as the income test for that tax year.

A homeowner can also be presumed to meet the income limit by enrolling in one of these programs:

  • Aid to the Aged, Blind or Disabled
  • The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program
  • The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program
  • The Benefit Access program
  • The Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral Program

How and when do Illinois seniors apply?

The freeze needs a new Form PTAX-340 every year, filed with the chief county assessment office along with an affidavit of household income, age, marital status and who lived in the home on January 1. In counties under 3,000,000 people the statute sets July 1 of each taxable year as the filing date, and a county may pass an ordinance choosing a different date. In Cook County the chief county assessment officer announces the application period, and the Assessor's page says that after the normal filing period ends, late applications are processed as certificates of error.

For the basic senior exemption, filing rules vary by county. Some require Form PTAX-324 at first and Form PTAX-329 as an annual certificate. Ask your county assessor which form applies and when the window closes, since a county can publish its own deadline.

A few other rules matter for families:

  • A surviving spouse under 65 can receive the freeze for the year before and the year of the death if all other qualifications are met.
  • Married people living apart may claim the exemption for only one residence.
  • In counties under 3,000,000 people, a physician's statement can extend a missed deadline by up to 3 months.

What happens to these exemptions when an Illinois home is sold or the owner dies?

Each exemption is tied to a qualifying person living in the home, so a buyer applies for any exemption on the buyer's own eligibility. Cook County's Assessor explains that if a parent who lived in the home on January 1 passes away, the property still qualifies for that year, and the son or daughter submits the application with a death certificate, identification and any letters of office or power of attorney paperwork.

A homeowner who is moving to assisted living keeps the freeze in later years when the spouse still occupies the home, or when the home sits unoccupied but still belongs to the qualified person. The same carry forward language appears in section 15-170 for the basic exemption.

How does the Illinois senior tax deferral work?

The deferral lets a person 65 or older postpone all or part of the real estate taxes and special assessments on the principal residence. The Department of Revenue compares it to a loan against the property's market value: the state pays the taxes and later recovers the money, plus annual interest set by the Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral Act. Repayment comes when the property is sold or transferred, within one year of the taxpayer's death, or 90 days after the property stops qualifying.

The deferred amount, with interest and lien fees, cannot go past 80 percent of the taxpayer's equity in the property. Under 320 ILCS 30/4, the collector records a statement with the county recorder that becomes a lien on the real estate for the deferred taxes plus accrued interest. Applications use Forms IL-1017 and IL-1018, available from the county treasurer's or collector's office; ask that office for the income limit and the filing deadline that apply.

For a seller, the lien matters at closing because the deferral comes due on sale. A payoff figure from the county office before listing shows how much of the sale price goes toward it.

More questions about Illinois Senior Exemption and Senior Freeze

What is the senior freeze income limit in Illinois?

$75,000 of household income for taxable year 2026, which is payable in 2027. The limit moves to $77,000 for 2027 and $79,000 for 2028 and after.

Do I have to reapply for the senior exemption every year in Cook County?

No for the basic Senior Exemption, which the Assessor's office renews automatically once granted. Yes for the Senior Freeze, which must be filed every year.

How old do I have to be for the Illinois senior exemption?

You must be 65 or older during the taxable year. Under section 15-170, a person who will turn 65 during the assessment year can apply that year.

Does the senior freeze stop my property tax bill from rising?

No. It holds the equalized assessed value at the base amount. The bill can still go up if tax rates rise or if improvements added to the home increase its value.

When must a senior tax deferral be repaid in Illinois?

When the property is sold or transferred, within one year of the taxpayer's death, or 90 days after the property ceases to qualify for the program.

Illinois estate tax FAQ

Does Illinois have an inheritance tax?

We did not confirm an Illinois inheritance tax on an official page. Illinois does impose an estate tax; check with the Attorney General estate tax page.

Does Illinois charge an estate tax or an inheritance tax?

Illinois charges an estate tax, paid by the estate before assets reach the heirs. It does not tax what each heir receives. The Attorney General's estate tax page mentions an Illinois inheritance tax only in one context: a release may be needed when the decedent died before January 1, 1983. For deaths since then, the question is whether the estate itself crosses the Illinois threshold.

The tax is governed by the Illinois Estate and Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax Act, 35 ILCS 405. The Attorney General administers it, takes the returns, and publishes a new set of forms and instructions for each year of death. The current listing on the Attorney General's site covers decedents who died from 2023 through 2026.

What is the Illinois estate tax threshold?

The Illinois exclusion amount is $4,000,000. Section 2 of the Act sets that figure for persons dying on or after January 1, 2013, after lower amounts of $2,000,000 for deaths before 2012 and $3,500,000 for deaths in 2012. The Attorney General's instruction sheet stresses that the exclusion operates as a taxable threshold and not as a credit against tax.

When the gross value of an estate, after adding adjusted taxable gifts, exceeds $4,000,000, an Illinois Form 700 must be filed. That requirement applies whether or not a federal return is due. For 2023 deaths the instruction sheet gives the federal exemption as $12,920,000, so an estate can owe Illinois tax while owing nothing federally.

  • Form 700 is the Illinois Estate and Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax Return.
  • It is filed with a federal Form 706 and its schedules, or with the same information in an alternate format if the estate is not federally taxable.
  • Wills, trusts, appraisals and attachments go in with the return.
  • For 2023 decedents the tax uses an interrelated calculation, and the Attorney General's online calculator takes the amounts from Lines 3 and 5 of Schedule A or B.

How does the Illinois estate tax behave near the threshold?

Because the $4,000,000 line is a threshold and not a credit, the tax can rise quickly just above it. The Attorney General's 2023 sheet prints worked results for several estates. They are examples for 2023 decedents, and the sheet should be consulted for the year of death in question.

The sheet notes that Florida imposes no state estate tax, so the Illinois share still applies in the last row. For a decedent who lived outside Illinois, a preliminary tax is figured as if all assets were in Illinois, then multiplied by the ratio of Illinois assets to total assets. A house in Illinois therefore sits in the Illinois share of an out-of-state owner's estate.

When is the Illinois estate tax due, and where is it filed?

The tax is due nine months after the date of death. Extensions are available on application to the Attorney General, and the Attorney General also recognizes federal extensions. An application for an Attorney General extension goes in on Form 700-EXT, or as a written explanation of why on-time filing or payment is impossible or impractical, and it should be filed within nine months of death.

  • Payment of tax, interest and penalties goes directly to the Illinois State Treasurer, using the Treasurer's estate tax payment form. It does not go to a county.
  • Original returns for Cook, DuPage, Lake and McHenry counties, with a copy of the federal return, go to the Estate Tax Section at the Attorney General's Chicago office. All other counties file with the Springfield office at 500 South Second Street.
  • Questions can go to the Estate Tax Section: (312) 814-2491 in Chicago or (217) 524-5095 in Springfield.
  • If federal tax is paid in installments, the Illinois tax may be paid in installments too, using the worksheet on Form 4350a.

Form 700 also has a box to request a Certificate of Discharge, which an executor or heir may want to ask about before relying on the estate being closed out.

What do marital deductions and civil unions mean for Illinois estate tax?

For deaths on or after January 1, 2009, an estate can make an Illinois-only QTIP election on a timely filed Illinois return, separate from any federal election. The Attorney General's 2023 sheet gives an example in which a $12,920,000 estate with an Illinois QTIP election of $8,920,000 owes no Illinois tax. The election requires the surviving spouse's Social Security number and a list of the QTIP property.

Illinois treats civil union partners the same as spouses for the Illinois marital deduction, under 86 Ill. Adm. Code 2000.200. The same sheet warns that the unused federal exemption of a deceased spouse does not carry over for the Illinois computation, so portability does not help here.

Does the small estate affidavit let heirs sell an Illinois house?

No. The small estate affidavit in 755 ILCS 5/25-1 transfers personal property such as bank accounts, safe deposit contents and evidence of interest, not real estate. It may be used only when no letters of office are outstanding and no petition for letters is contemplated or pending anywhere, and the decedent's personal property is limited to $150,000, not counting motor vehicles registered with the Secretary of State.

A house therefore normally needs another route, which depends on how title was held and whether the estate goes through probate. The circuit clerk in the county where the decedent lived can explain what forms exist, and an estate attorney can say whether Form 700 and a Certificate of Discharge belong in the file before a sale is scheduled.

What should heirs do about an inherited Illinois house?

Start by adding up what the decedent owned, including the house, accounts and any adjusted taxable gifts made during life, and compare the total with $4,000,000. If the estate is under that line, no Illinois return is required, though the county where the house sits still bills property tax each year. If it is over, calendar nine months from the date of death and contact the Estate Tax Section early.

  • Keep the death date and the appraisal handy, because Form 700 and the instruction sheet both turn on values.
  • Ask the county treasurer for the open property tax balance on the inherited parcel, and ask the county assessor about any exemption the decedent held.
  • Heirs who do not want to carry repairs, taxes and utilities on the house sometimes sell it as is to a cash buyer. The sale terms should deal with any open tax balance in writing.

Is there an Illinois inheritance tax?

No current inheritance tax appears on the Attorney General's estate tax page. The only inheritance tax reference there concerns releases that may be needed when the decedent died before January 1, 1983. Illinois does charge an estate tax on larger estates.

How much must an estate be worth before Illinois estate tax applies?

The exclusion amount is $4,000,000. If the estate's gross value plus adjusted taxable gifts exceeds that figure, Form 700 must be filed. The exclusion is a taxable threshold, not a credit.

When is Illinois estate tax due?

It is due nine months after the date of death. Extensions come from the Attorney General on Form 700-EXT or a written explanation filed within nine months, and federal extensions are recognized. Payment goes to the Illinois State Treasurer.

Who do I contact with Illinois estate tax questions?

The Estate Tax Section of the Illinois Attorney General's office. The Chicago number is (312) 814-2491 and the Springfield number is (217) 524-5095. The office posts forms for each year of death on its website.

Can I use a small estate affidavit to transfer a house in Illinois?

No. The affidavit under 755 ILCS 5/25-1 transfers personal property up to $150,000, excluding registered motor vehicles, and only when no letters of office are outstanding. Real estate needs a different process, so check with the circuit clerk or an estate attorney.

Illinois inheritance tax FAQ

Can I sell an inherited house in Illinois?

Yes, if you have authority to sign. Authority comes from the estate representative or from title that passed to you. Ask the title company.

Does Illinois tax a house you inherit?

The state tax that touches inherited property in Illinois is an estate tax, and it is charged to the estate of the person who died, not billed on a separate heir's return. The Illinois Department of Revenue answers a question about an inheritance or estate tax with a yes, adds that it does not administer the tax, and sends questions to the Office of the Attorney General.

For most families the practical question is whether the estate is large enough to owe anything. The Attorney General's fact sheet sets a taxable threshold, and the filing duty starts only when an estate's gross value passes it. A house that passes with other assets still counts toward that total, so add up the house, the accounts and any adjusted taxable gifts before deciding.

What is the Illinois estate tax threshold?

The Attorney General's instruction sheet for deaths in 2023 states that the exclusion amount for Illinois estate tax purposes is $4,000,000. It describes the figure as a taxable threshold and not a credit against the tax. If the gross value of an estate exceeds $4,000,000 after adjusted taxable gifts are added, an Illinois Form 700 must be filed, whether or not a federal return is required.

The Attorney General posts a separate fact sheet for each year of death, so read the one that matches the date of death. The sheet also says that the federal rule letting a surviving spouse carry over an unused exemption does not apply to the Illinois computation, and that a separate Illinois QTIP election is available to the estate for deaths since January 1, 2009.

  • Civil union partners recognized under Illinois law can claim the same marital deduction treatment for Illinois purposes, with additional filings.
  • The Attorney General offers an online estate tax calculator for the interrelated computation.
  • Estates that owe no federal tax may still have to file Form 700 with the Illinois Attorney General.

Who files the return, when is it due and where is it paid?

The estate representative files Form 700 with the Attorney General's Estate Tax Section, and the tax is due nine months after the date of death. The original return goes by mail, courier or hand delivery to the Chicago office for Cook, DuPage, Lake and McHenry counties, and to the Springfield office for every other county.

Payment is made separately to the Illinois State Treasurer using the Treasurer's estate tax payment form. Extensions are available: the Attorney General honors federal extensions, and a request for its own extension should be filed within nine months of death on Form 700-EXT or with a written explanation. If the federal tax is paid in installments, the Illinois tax may be paid in installments too.

Which taxes and costs apply when an heir sells the inherited house?

Selling the house triggers the same transfer charges as any sale. Section 31-15 sets the state transfer tax at 50¢ per $500, and the Department of Revenue notes that a county may add a 25¢ per $500 levy. Home rule municipalities can impose an additional transfer tax. Buyer and seller complete Form PTAX-203, the Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration, which goes to the county that holds the parcel and can be prepared through MyDec in participating counties.

If the property remains subject to a mortgage, only the owner's equity counts in the base, provided the deed states that on its face. Ask the county recorder of deeds what the local stamp or transfer tax is for your parcel, because counties and some municipalities differ.

Property tax keeps running while the estate is open. In Cook County, a parent who lived in the home on January 1 and used it as a principal residence leaves a property that is still eligible for the senior exemption for that year, and the heir applies using the death certificate and letters of office.

What if the person who died lived out of state but owned Illinois property?

The Attorney General's sheet covers both resident and non-resident decedents. The estate first computes a preliminary tax as if every asset were located in Illinois, then multiplies that figure by the ratio of Illinois assets to total assets to get the apportioned tax. An out-of-state owner of an Illinois house therefore still has to account for the house on Form 700 if the whole estate is above the threshold.

Questions about a specific estate go to the Estate Tax Section. The sheet lists (312) 814-2491 for the Chicago office and (217) 524-5095 for Springfield. Have the date of death, the value of all assets and a copy of any federal Form 706 ready before calling.

  • Gather appraisals for the house and any other real estate.
  • List where each asset is located, since the apportionment depends on it.
  • Keep wills, trusts and gift records together for the lawyer.

Who has the authority to sell an inherited house in Illinois?

The person with court-issued letters of office, or an heir who already holds title through a joint tenancy, trust or Transfer on Death Instrument, can sign. Letters of office are the court papers that prove the personal representative's power, and banks and title companies ask to see them before changing title to property held only in the decedent's name.

An independent representative acting for the estate may sell real estate at public or private sale without a court order, though real estate specifically left to a named legatee cannot be sold without that legatee's written consent (755 ILCS 5/28-8). A small estate affidavit does not reach a house. The Illinois Legal Aid page lists a house as outside the affidavit process.

  • Joint tenancy with right of survivorship: title passes to the surviving owner.
  • Trust property: the trustee signs under the trust document.
  • Property only in the decedent's name: letters of office are needed.

What should an heir do before talking to buyers?

Start by finding out how title is held and whether a will exists. A will must be filed with the circuit court clerk right after death under 755 ILCS 5/6-1, and a person who willfully hides one for 30 days after learning of the death faces felony penalties. Then speak with an Illinois lawyer about whether an estate must be opened, since only a licensed Illinois lawyer can start a probate case.

Gather the death certificate, the deed, the latest property tax bill and any mortgage statement. If the decedent's estate may approach $4,000,000, ask the lawyer to check Form 700 first. A cash buyer can close after the estate representative is authorized to sign, so the legal steps usually set the timeline, not the buyer.

More questions about Illinois Inheritance Tax

Is there an Illinois inheritance tax bill for heirs?

The tax Illinois administers on death is an estate tax, handled by the Attorney General and paid by the estate. The Department of Revenue says it does not administer inheritance or estate tax and points questions to the Attorney General.

How large must an estate be to owe Illinois estate tax?

The Attorney General's 2023 sheet gives a $4,000,000 taxable threshold. Gross value above that after adjusted taxable gifts requires Form 700. Check the fact sheet for the actual year of death.

When must the Illinois estate tax be paid?

It is due nine months after the date of death, payable to the State Treasurer. Extensions can be requested within nine months, and federal extensions are honored.

Does transfer tax apply to an estate sale?

Yes, the sale carries the usual transfer tax: 50¢ per $500 at the state level, a possible county levy, and in some home rule municipalities a local one.

Is a sale possible before the estate closes?

Possibly. An independent representative with letters of office may sell real estate without a court order, except property specifically left to a legatee needs that person's written consent. Title held in joint tenancy or a trust follows its own rules.

Illinois small estate affidavit FAQ

What is the small estate limit?

The limit is $150,000 in personal property under 755 ILCS 5/25-1 as amended, according to the statute text the research opened.

What is a small estate affidavit in Illinois?

It is a sworn statement that lets a person holding a dead person's money or property release it to the heirs without a court case. Section 25-1 of the Probate Act of 1975, 755 ILCS 5/25-1, tells a bank, a transfer agent or anyone owing the decedent money to pay or deliver to the people named in a conforming affidavit. The holder who acts in good faith on a copy that substantially follows the statutory form is protected as if the payment had gone to a court appointed representative.

The key phrase for homeowners is "personal property." The affidavit covers cash, accounts, safe deposit contents and similar items, and it does not cover the house.

What is the Illinois small estate affidavit limit?

The limit is $150,000 in tangible and intangible personal property, not counting motor vehicles registered with the Secretary of State. That figure comes from Public Act 104-346, effective August 15, 2025, and applies to a decedent who died on or after that date. A second amendment, Public Act 104-624, takes effect January 1, 2027 and leaves the $150,000 figure alone while listing vehicle types that no longer count as excluded vehicles.

Source: 755 ILCS 5/25-1, subsection (a-5).

If the affidavit is used only to retitle vehicles with the Secretary of State, it can transfer them without regard to the value of the personal estate.

Can an Illinois small estate affidavit transfer a house?

No. The statute speaks of transferring personal property, and Illinois Legal Aid Online says plainly that the affidavit cannot be used to transfer real property such as a house. It adds that the decedent's real estate may already have passed by a Transfer on Death Instrument or by joint tenancy, in which case the affidavit can still handle the rest of the estate.

When the house is titled in the decedent's name alone, the usual route runs through the circuit court. Under 755 ILCS 5/20-1, a representative appointed by the court takes possession of the decedent's real estate during administration, collects rents, keeps the buildings in repair, pays taxes and liens and may insure the property. Subsection (d) leaves intact the representative's power to sell or mortgage real estate under the Probate Act.

What conditions must be met before using the affidavit?

Subsection (a-5) sets two gates. No letters of office can be outstanding on the estate, and no petition for letters can be contemplated or pending in Illinois or any other jurisdiction. The decedent's personal estate passing by intestacy or under a will must stay within the dollar limit. The affiant also attaches a copy of the death certificate, and a certified copy of the will if one was filed.

A person who holds a will must file it with the clerk of the proper county right after the testator dies, under 755 ILCS 5/6-1. Hiding a will for 30 days after learning of the death is sentenced as a Class 3 felony. The affidavit is signed before a notary under penalty of perjury, and an out of state affiant names an Illinois agent for service of process.

Illinois Legal Aid Online says the form can be downloaded from the Secretary of State's website or picked up at the circuit clerk's office, and it suggests making at least two copies of the signed affidavit to show to each bank or company holding property of the estate. A holder who refuses to turn the property over can be taken to civil court.

Items the affidavit must list include:

  • The affiant's addresses and relationship to the decedent
  • The decedent's name, date of death and last residence
  • Each asset with its fair market value and every registered vehicle
  • Known unpaid debts by class, or a statement that all debts were paid
  • The surviving spouse, minor children and adult dependent children
  • The heirs or legatees and each share

Who gets paid first from an Illinois small estate?

Creditors come before heirs. Paragraph 7.5 of the affidavit says every valid claim must be paid from the estate before anything goes to an heir or legatee, and if a class cannot be paid in full, its claims are paid pro rata. The affiant also agrees to indemnify creditors, heirs and anyone relying on the affidavit for losses caused by the affiant's act or omission, with attorney's fees owed to a person who recovers.

The statutory order of classes is:

  • Class 1: funeral and burial expenses, administration expenses and statutory custodial claims
  • Class 2: the surviving spouse's or child's award
  • Class 3: debts due the United States
  • Class 4: wages owed employees, up to $800 per claimant, for services within 4 months before death, and last illness expenses
  • Class 5: money or property held in trust that cannot be identified or traced
  • Class 6: debts due the State of Illinois and local governments in Illinois
  • Class 7: all other claims

The award for a surviving spouse who was an Illinois resident is $20,000 plus $10,000 for each minor or adult dependent child who lived with the spouse at the time of death. With no spouse, the same amount goes to those children in equal shares.

How does selling an inherited Illinois home work when the affidavit does not apply?

The seller needs legal authority first. If the home is in the decedent's name alone, an heir cannot sign a deed on the strength of an affidavit, so the sale waits for a court appointed representative or another transfer of title. Ask the clerk of the circuit court in the county where the decedent lived what filings the probate division requires, and ask the county recorder what proof of authority it expects with a deed.

Under section 20-1, a representative may not take possession of the portion of real estate occupied as a residence by the heir or legatee unless the will says so or the court finds possession is necessary for claims, administration costs, taxes, preservation or distribution. The court may also hand possession to an heir or legatee on petition if the property will not be needed to pay debts.

The affidavit can still handle bank accounts and vehicles while the house moves through probate, which keeps the two tracks separate. Taxes, insurance and upkeep on the house continue in the meantime, and the representative carries those duties.

More questions about Illinois Small Estate Affidavit

What is the small estate limit in Illinois?

$150,000 in personal property, not counting motor vehicles registered with the Secretary of State, under 755 ILCS 5/25-1 as amended by Public Act 104-346.

Can I sell my parent's house with a small estate affidavit?

No. The affidavit transfers personal property only. A house titled in the decedent's name usually needs a court appointed representative before it can be sold, unless it already passed by a Transfer on Death Instrument or joint tenancy.

Do I have to pay the decedent's debts before giving heirs their share?

Yes. The affiant must pay valid claims in the statutory order before any distribution to an heir or legatee, and signs an indemnity for losses caused by the affiant's acts or omissions.

How much is the spouse or child award in an Illinois small estate?

$20,000 for the surviving spouse plus $10,000 for each minor or adult dependent child who lived with the spouse at death. With no spouse, that sum is divided equally among the children.

Does a small estate affidavit need a notary?

Yes. The form is signed and sworn before a notary public under penalty of perjury, and a fraudulent statement is perjury under section 32-2 of the Criminal Code of 2012.

How does probate work in Illinois?

Probate is the court process that settles a dead person's affairs: a personal representative gathers the property, pays valid debts and expenses, and gives what is left to the people entitled to it. With a valid will the estate is distributed under the will, and without one Illinois inheritance law decides who receives what. A person named in the will is called the executor, and a court-appointed representative when there is no will is called the administrator.

A case opens in the circuit court of the county where the decedent lived. Illinois Legal Aid Online says an Illinois-licensed lawyer must file the case, because the estate is a separate legal entity that cannot represent itself, and that a family member who tries to file alone will be told to hire a lawyer.

When does a house have to go through probate?

Probate is usually needed when the person owned real estate in their name alone and nothing moves it automatically at death. A house held in joint tenancy with survivorship, held in a trust, or covered by a recorded Transfer on Death Instrument passes outside probate. A will alone does not avoid probate, because the court still appoints the executor and gives that person authority.

For a surviving spouse, a jointly owned home normally becomes the survivor's property. If the house was only in the deceased spouse's name, probate may still be needed. The title company decides what it needs to insure a sale, so ask it early which documents it will accept.

  • Sole name, no beneficiary designation: probate is usually required.
  • Joint tenancy with survivorship: passes to the surviving owner.
  • Trust or Transfer on Death Instrument: follows the instrument.

What are the steps from filing to closing the estate?

The lawyer files a petition in the right county. With a will, the petition asks the court to admit it and name the executor, and the court will not look at the petition until the will itself is on file. The law requires whoever holds a will to file it with the clerk right after death. Once the court is satisfied, it appoints the representative and issues letters of office.

Then come notices to creditors, collecting and protecting the property, paying debts and expenses, and distribution. Illinois does not use one statewide form set, so the circuit clerk of the county supplies the petitions and notices.

What does independent administration allow?

Under Article 28 an executor or administrator can administer the estate without a court order or filings, except where the Article or an interested person asks for court involvement. An independent representative who acts reasonably for the estate's best interests may lease, mortgage, or sell the decedent's real estate at public or private sale, for cash or on credit, without asking the judge.

One limit matters for a sale: real estate that the will specifically leaves to a named person cannot be leased, sold or mortgaged without that person's written consent. A representative can also confirm title in an heir or legatee by recording an instrument that releases the estate's interest.

Any interested person can petition to end independent status. The court must grant it unless the will directs independent administration, in which case it needs good cause, or the petitioner is a creditor or a legatee other than a residuary legatee, in which case it must find that termination is necessary to protect that person. After termination, the representative follows the rules for supervised administration.

How do creditor claims affect the timing of a sale?

Creditors have a set window to file. The published notice states a claim date no earlier than six months after the first publication or three months after the notice is mailed or delivered, whichever is later. A claim not filed by that date is barred, and in any event claims are barred two years after death.

A representative who gives proper notice in good faith is not personally liable to a creditor, but a claim that is not barred can still be pursued against assets that have not been distributed and against a distributee, up to the amount the distributee received above what they would have gotten had the claim been paid. The bar does not cut off actions to establish the decedent's liability to the extent liability insurance covers it.

What happens if there is no will?

A person who dies without a valid will is intestate, and Illinois law picks the heirs. Property may go to a surviving spouse, children, parents or other relatives as the statute sets out, which can differ from what the person would have chosen. The court names an administrator, who has the same duties as an executor: collect assets, pay debts and expenses, and distribute the rest.

If you find a will after the case starts, take it to the lawyer at once and file it with the clerk. The Probate Act makes it a Class 3 felony to willfully alter or destroy a will without the testator's direction, or to hide one for 30 days after learning of the death.

  • Locate the original will, not a copy.
  • Ask the title company what proof of authority it wants, since title companies often need to see the letters of office.
  • Keep a list of every parcel the decedent owned, because each deed may need its own recording.

Can a small estate skip probate?

Some estates can skip it, though a house rules out the shortcut. Illinois Legal Aid Online says a small estate affidavit may be used only if the estate has no real estate, at least 60 days have passed since the death, no probate petition is filed or pending, and total personal property is $150,000 or less. Registered motor vehicles are listed on the affidavit but do not count toward the cap.

The statute, 755 ILCS 5/25-1, also requires that the affiant pay valid claims before distributing to heirs. The affidavit transfers personal property such as accounts, not land. A homeowner heir should plan for either a probate case, a trust, a Transfer on Death Instrument, or joint title to move a house.

  • Check how the deed reads before assuming probate is needed.
  • Ask the circuit clerk in the county of death for forms and local steps.
  • Illinois Legal Aid Online lists a free application for people who cannot afford a lawyer.

More questions about Illinois Probate Process

Do I need a lawyer to open probate in Illinois?

Yes. Illinois Legal Aid Online says an Illinois-licensed lawyer must open the case, and the court will pause a case filed by a family member until counsel is found.

Can an executor sell the house during probate?

Often yes. An independent representative may sell real estate without a court order under 755 ILCS 5/28-8, but property specifically left to a legatee needs that person's written consent.

How long do creditors have to file claims?

The notice sets a date at least six months after first publication or three months after mailing, whichever is later. All claims are barred two years after death regardless of letters (755 ILCS 5/18-3 and 18-12).

Does a will avoid probate in Illinois?

No. A will names who gets the property and often names the executor, but if the property must pass through probate the court still appoints the executor and gives that person authority.

Which court handles an Illinois probate case?

The circuit court in the county where the decedent lived. Forms and filing steps differ by county, so the circuit clerk's office or website is where to look.

What does an Illinois quitclaim deed actually transfer?

An Illinois quitclaim deed passes to the grantee whatever interest the grantor holds on the day of signing, and nothing beyond that. Under 765 ILCS 5/10, a deed in the statutory form is a good conveyance, release and quit claim of "all the then existing legal or equitable rights of the grantor" in the described premises. Title the grantor picks up afterward stays behind unless the deed adds words expressing that intention.

That limit explains where the form gets used in Illinois. It suits transfers between people who already know the ownership history, such as co-owners or relatives. A buyer from the open market gets only what the seller owns, and the statutory form contains no promise about the quality of the title.

What does the Illinois statutory quitclaim form say?

The form names the grantor and the consideration, then says the grantor will "convey and quit claim" to the grantee "all interest" in the described real estate in a named county, followed by a date and signature. The statute asks that party names be typed or printed under the signatures and that the page leave a blank space of 3 1/2 inches by 3 1/2 inches for the recorder. Leaving out either detail does not affect the validity of the deed.

A deed drawn on this pattern normally carries these items:

  • The grantor's name and place of residence
  • The grantee's name or names
  • The consideration stated in the deed
  • The property's legal description plus the Illinois county where it sits
  • The date and the grantor's signature

What must be filed with a deed at the Illinois recorder?

A transfer declaration has to go in with the deed. The rule sits in section 31-25 of the Property Tax Code: the declaration is presented with the deed, or within 3 business days after the transfer takes effect, whichever is earlier. One seller and one buyer, or their attorneys or agents, must sign. Apart from deeds covered by section 31-45, a recorder turns away any deed that arrives alone.

The form asks for the stated value, the parcel number, the legal description, the type of deed, the address, whether the parties are related and any homestead exemptions shown on the latest tax bill. According to the state revenue agency's own transfer tax page that Form PTAX-203 can be completed in MyDec when the county participates, and that other counties use fill-in forms. Once the deed is on record, section 31-30 sends the declaration on to the assessor's office, which is how the sale price reaches the county.

How much is the Illinois transfer tax on a quitclaim deed?

Illinois taxes the privilege of transferring title at a rate of fifty cents per $500 block of the value shown on the declaration, with any leftover fraction counted as a full block, according to 35 ILCS 200/31-10. If the document states that the property passes subject to a mortgage, the unpaid mortgage balance comes out of the tax base. Liability exists even when no document is recorded.

Local layers can sit on top. The Cook County Clerk's transfer fees page prints the state and county rates below, and lets a user look up any municipality in Cook. Outside Cook, call the recorder for the county and ask which local rates apply.

Which Illinois deeds are exempt from transfer tax?

Section 31-45 lists the exempt deeds and trust documents. Several of them come up with quitclaims:

  • Deeds where the actual consideration is less than $100
  • Deeds that confirm, correct, modify or supplement a deed already recorded, with no additional consideration
  • Deeds of partition
  • Deeds issued to a mortgage holder in foreclosure or in a transfer in lieu of foreclosure
  • Tax deeds
  • Deeds that release property held as security for a debt

Exempt does not always mean excused from paperwork. For some categories, including actual exchanges of real estate, the statute says the deed is still not exempt from filing the declaration.

What does Cook County charge to record an Illinois deed?

Cook County prices a deed, listed as Document Class 1, at $107. The Clerk's recording fee page splits that into a $55 county recording fee, a $23 GIS fee, a $10 document storage fee, an $18 State Rental Housing Support Fee and a $1 non-government filer fee. Filers not subject to the state fee pay $19 less. Recording by mail with return adds $5 per document.

Public Act 104-40, effective January 1, 2026, adds a fee exemption to section 10: a quitclaim recorded only to reflect a legal name change, where one individual or the same group appears on both sides, pays no recording fees. Fee schedules in other Illinois counties are set locally, so ask the county recorder before mailing a deed.

Where does the transfer declaration go once the deed is on file?

Section 31-30 says the recorder never records the declaration itself. The deed's document number is written on it, and a copy travels to the county assessor or supervisor of assessments inside 30 days of receipt. That office adds the latest assessed value for each parcel, then forwards the batch to the state revenue agency by a deadline tied either to receipt or to the close of the prior year's appeal session, whichever is later.

The assessor may keep a copy to help decide the proper valuation of the transferred property and of other parcels in the county. A quitclaim between relatives for a stated price of a few dollars therefore still leaves a record at the assessor's office, and the figures on the declaration should match the deed.

Does a quitclaim deed work when you want to sell an Illinois house?

It works when the person signing actually owns the interest being sold, because the buyer receives only that interest. Before you sign, ask whichever title company runs the closing which deed form it will take for your Illinois property.

Gather these for the recorder:

  • The signed and dated deed with the blank space reserved for the recorder
  • The completed transfer declaration, signed by a seller and a buyer or their agents
  • The transfer tax, where the transfer is not exempt
  • The county recording fee

An owner selling an inherited or jointly held house as it stands can raise the deed question early with the buyer's side, so the paperwork is settled well ahead of closing day.

More questions about Illinois Quitclaim Deed

How does an Illinois quitclaim differ from a warranty deed?

It differs in what it carries. The statutory quitclaim form conveys the grantor's then existing legal or equitable rights, and it does not extend to title acquired later unless the deed adds words saying so. The statute for the quitclaim form contains no promise about the quality of title.

Who pays transfer tax on an Illinois quitclaim deed?

The Cook County Clerk's table lists the seller as the party liable for both the state and the Cook County tax. Outside Cook, contact the county recorder to learn who is liable and whether a local tax applies.

Is the transfer tax owed if the deed is never recorded?

Yes. Section 31-10 says the tax is due whether or not a document is recorded, and it applies to transfers made through one or several related transactions.

Can I record a quitclaim deed just to change the name on my title?

Yes. The recording carries no recording fees when the sole purpose is to reflect a legal name change and the grantor is also the grantee under a new name. The exemption comes from Public Act 104-40, effective January 1, 2026.

How soon must the transfer declaration be filed?

With the deed, or within 3 business days after the transfer takes effect, whichever is earlier. The declaration needs a signature from at least one seller and one buyer, or their attorneys or agents.

Illinois transfer tax FAQ

Who pays the Chicago transfer tax?

Chicago says the buyer pays $3.75 per $500 and the seller pays $1.50 per $500 for the CTA portion.

What is the Illinois transfer tax on a home sale?

The state levies a stamp of 50 cents on every $500 block, or part of a block, of the value written on the transfer declaration (35 ILCS 200/31-10). The tax applies to deeds, to beneficial interests in a land trust and to controlling interests in a real estate entity. Liability does not depend on recording, and a series of related transactions is treated as one transfer.

Counties may add a second layer and a few cities add a third. A seller's closing statement therefore shows the state stamp plus any county or municipal charge. Chicago is the best known example of a city layer,.

Nothing in the statute tells the two sides how to divide the cost. Whatever your sales agreement says about stamps controls, so read that paragraph with your closing attorney or title agent before signing.

How do the state, county and Chicago layers compare?

Each layer counts value in blocks of $500, and the charge per block differs. The table shows only rates as the official pages print them.

The county tax comes from 55 ILCS 5/5-1031. The recorder or registrar of titles collects it ahead of recording, and it sits on top of every other privilege tax imposed by the state or a municipality. Ask the county recorder whether your county has adopted it.

Who collects the tax, and when is it paid?

The county recorder or registrar of titles collects the state tax. Under 35 ILCS 200/31-15, paper revenue stamps were to be phased out by December 31, 2025, and counties now issue electronic stamps or another electronic mark. Each recorder files a return with the Department of Revenue and remits the money by the 10th of the following month.

A deed cannot be accepted for recording until the stamps in the right amount have been bought, unless the deed is exempt. The recorder may affix the stamp before or after recording at the grantee's request. Ask your closing agent how the stamps are ordered and paid from the settlement funds.

  • The tax is computed from the value stated on the declaration, not from the assessed value on the tax bill.
  • The declaration goes to the recorder with the deed, or within 3 business days after the transfer, whichever comes first.
  • The Department of Revenue's MyDec system accepts the state forms and Chicago's Form 7551. Counties outside MyDec use fill-in PDF forms.

Which Illinois transfers are exempt from the state transfer tax?

Section 31-45 sets out the exempt instruments, and a few of them touch owners in financial trouble. Lenders who take a deed after foreclosure or through a deed-in-lieu pay no state stamp, and the same is true of tax deeds. Instruments given as security for a debt, instruments releasing that security and partition deeds are also on the list. For some exempt transfers a declaration must still go to the recorder.

  • Transfers made for actual consideration below $100.
  • Corrective or confirming deeds that add no new consideration to an earlier recorded deed.
  • Transfers involving government bodies and qualifying charitable, religious or educational groups, where the declaration is still required.
  • True exchanges of real estate, with any boot paid in money taxable.
  • Principal residence purchases under the Home Ownership Made Easy Act, again with a declaration.

Nothing is exempt automatically. The deed or the declaration must cite the exemption that fits, and the recorder can tell you how your county wants that notation worded.

What does Form PTAX-203 ask a seller to report?

Illinois uses Form PTAX-203, its transfer declaration, on most sales. One seller and one buyer, or their agents, sign it. State assessment studies draw on the answers, so the form collects more than a price.

  • The full actual consideration, excluding credits or refunds for repairs and improvements.
  • Personal property in the sale. An itemized list is required when personal property on a residence exceeds 5 percent of the price.
  • Whether the buyer plans to live there, and whether an agent, a sign or an ad was used to sell.
  • Special circumstances such as a court-ordered sale (including probate and foreclosure), a short sale, a bank-owned resale or a seller or buyer that is a financial institution.
  • The homestead exemption dollar amounts printed on the latest tax bill.

Willfully falsifying or leaving out required information is a Class B misdemeanor for a first offense under the Department's instructions. A buyer who knowingly gives a false grantee identity in Cook County faces its own misdemeanor charge. Sellers should check the form for accuracy before signing, even when the title company prepares it.

How does the Chicago transfer tax work for a seller?

Chicago imposes its tax on transferring title or a beneficial interest in real property in the city, whether or not the contract was signed in Chicago. The official page for Form 7551 gives $3.75 per $500 for the City portion and $1.50 per $500 for the CTA portion on transfers on or after April 1, 2008, for a combined $5.25. In general the buyer is responsible for $3.75 and the seller for $1.50.

The Department of Finance page lists exemptions that include transfers to lenders in foreclosure or in lieu of foreclosure, tax deeds, deeds securing debt, transfers under $500, and a court-ordered transfer of a primary residence between members of a couple in a divorce or legal separation. No transfer is exempt unless the declaration describes the facts and attaches support.

A refund of the CTA portion is available to a transferee who is 65 or older, occupies the home as a personal dwelling for at least a year, and bought at $250,000 or less. That refund is claimed by the buyer through the Tax Division, so it does not change what a Chicago seller owes.

How do mortgages, probate and as-is sales affect the tax?

If the deed states that title passes subject to a mortgage, the balance still outstanding drops out of the taxable basis. The PTAX-203 has a separate line for that amount, which makes the deed wording important, and your closing attorney can say which wording fits.

A sale by an estate is stamped like any other sale. The form includes a court-ordered sale box that covers probate. A lender that takes title by foreclosure deed or deed in lieu pays no state stamp. The lender's later resale is an ordinary sale and is reported on the form's bank REO line.

Selling as is leaves the tax unchanged. The declared price is what was actually paid, and the instructions exclude amounts credited or refunded to the buyer for repairs, so keep any written repair credit in the closing file.

What should an Illinois seller do before closing?

Confirm the transfer tax line early so it holds no surprises when you sign.

  • Call the recorder to learn whether the county levies its own tax and what proof of exemption the office takes.
  • Match each layer to the payer named in your sales agreement.
  • Read the draft PTAX-203 line by line, starting with price, personal property and the special-circumstance boxes.
  • For a Chicago address, ask for the Form 7551 total and each side's share.
  • File a copy of the signed declaration with your closing papers.

The steps are the same for a direct as-is cash sale and for a listed sale: one declaration, one recorder, the same stamp.

More questions about Illinois Transfer Tax

What is the Illinois state transfer tax rate?

Fifty cents per $500 block, rounded up for any partial block, based on the value stated in the declaration (35 ILCS 200/31-10). Counties may add 25 cents per $500, and Chicago adds its own tax.

Who pays the transfer tax in Illinois?

The statute does not say, so the sales agreement controls. Chicago's official page says the buyer generally owes $3.75 of its $5.25 per $500 and the seller $1.50.

Does a foreclosure deed or tax deed owe transfer tax?

Neither does. Both appear on the section 31-45 exemption list. Whether a declaration is needed depends on the exemption, so the recorder can confirm.

When is the declaration due?

Illinois counties sell delinquent property tax at annual tax sales, and owners can redeem during a statutory period.

What the official sources say

  • Scavenger sale redemption for sales on/after Sept 9, 1993: penalty interest of 3% per month (first 2 months), 12% (2-6 months), 24% (6-12), 36% (12-18), 48% (18-24), then 48% plus 6% per year, on taxes/costs due; non-owner-occupied-single-family redemptions also require payment of other delinquent taxes. (35 ILCS 200/21-260(f); source)

What we could not confirm

  • Tax deed procedure under 35 ILCS 200/22-30 was not opened.

Illinois tax sales FAQ

How long is the redemption period?

For certificates issued on or after January 1, 2024, residential property has 3 years under 35 ILCS 200/21-350, with shorter periods for some property types.

How does an Illinois tax sale work?

An Illinois tax sale auctions the unpaid property tax on a parcel, not the house itself. After taxes turn delinquent, the county collector must publish a notice of the intended application for judgment and sale, and the notice lists each delinquent property by PIN number and, where available, by address (35 ILCS 200/21-110). The notice runs in a newspaper published in the township or road district, or in a county newspaper when none exists there.

Bidders compete on the penalty. Under 35 ILCS 200/21-215, the person offering to pay the amount due for the least penalty percentage becomes the purchaser, and no bid may exceed a 9% penalty on the tax. The winner receives a certificate of purchase, and the owner keeps title while the redemption clock runs.

A county board may also bid as trustee for the taxing districts, applying the unpaid taxes to the bid so that no cash changes hands (35 ILCS 200/21-90). A county that holds a certificate this way can later sell the property or assign the certificate to a municipality, a land bank or a nonprofit housing developer.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Illinois house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How long does an owner have to redeem?

Property sold at a tax sale may be redeemed any time before 3 years from the date of sale, with listed exceptions, under 35 ILCS 200/21-350. The first exception concerns property that is vacant on the date of sale. The section says the 2024 changes apply to certificates issued on or after January 1, 2024, and the 104th General Assembly amendment applies to certificates issued on or after July 10, 2026.

Because the rule depends on the issue date of the certificate, an older sale may run on a shorter schedule. The county clerk can tell you the sale date and the redemption deadline for any parcel. Every redemption period begins on the date of the tax sale, according to section 22-5.

The buyer can lengthen the period by filing a written notice with the county clerk, but only to a date no later than 3 years after the sale, and only with the clerk's date-stamped acknowledgment (35 ILCS 200/21-385). For certificates a county holds as trustee, the clerk may set up a payment plan that waives interest penalties while the owner keeps up with it.

What does it cost to redeem?

You pay the county clerk, not the tax buyer. Section 21-355 requires a deposit in United States money, a cashier's check, a certified check or a qualifying money order payable to the county clerk. It counts as timely only if the clerk's office receives it in person before the close of business on the last day, or if a post office cancellation mark is dated at least one day earlier.

The total has several parts: the certificate amount, an accrued penalty, any later taxes the buyer paid plus a 12% penalty for each year or part of a year, and fees tied to the buyer's court filings and notices. The penalty is a multiple of the penalty bid at the sale, and it steps up every six months.

Accrued penalty by redemption date, from 35 ILCS 200/21-355(b)
Redeemed withinPenalty equals certificate amount times
6 months of the sale1 times the penalty bid
6 to 12 months2 times the penalty bid
12 to 18 months3 times the penalty bid
18 to 24 months4 times the penalty bid
24 to 30 months5 times the penalty bid
30 to 36 months6 times the penalty bid

Ask the clerk for a written redemption figure for the exact day you plan to pay, because the number moves as periods change and as fees are posted.

What notices must a tax buyer send before asking for a deed?

The law makes the tax buyer prove that the owner was warned. Within 4 months and 15 days after the sale, the buyer delivers a notice to the county clerk, who mails it by registered or certified mail to the party in whose name the taxes were last assessed (35 ILCS 200/22-5). The form tells the owner that title and the right to possession may transfer, that a homeowner could eventually face eviction, and that HUD can point to local housing counselors.

  • Between 6 and 3 months before the redemption period ends, the buyer gives a second notice to owners, occupants, the municipality and interested parties such as a mortgagee of record (section 22-10).
  • The petition for a tax deed is filed in circuit court between 6 and 3 months before the period expires (section 22-30).
  • The notice names a hearing date and says the owner may respond or appear and speak to the court.
  • The court is told to insist on strict compliance with sections 22-10 through 22-25.

A missed or defective notice is a real defense, so keep every envelope and letter you receive and give copies to an attorney.
