What happens when the redemption period ends?

Since the 2024 amendments, a court that finds the notices proper orders a judicial tax deed auction, and the property is offered to the highest bidder within 120 days of the order (35 ILCS 200/22-40). The tax deed judgment amount includes the redemption figure, the petitioner's later taxes and costs, a capped attorney fee and publication costs. It earns interest at 0.75% per month from the judgment until the auction.

The former owner is not automatically wiped out. The statutory notice tells an owner that money left after taxes and fees are paid may be claimed, and the clerk's tax deed fee comes with a surplus equity fund fee of $500 in counties under 3,000,000 residents and $1,000 in larger ones. Those fees fund the county's surplus equity fund. Deeds issued to a county trustee skip that fee.

A tax deed does not erase every claim, since section 22-45 lets a court void a deed in limited cases. In counties of 3,000,000 or more, a homestead deed can be voided on petition within 3 months of the order if the home was owner occupied and a county employee made a negligent or willful error that the owner relied on.

What is a scavenger sale?

A scavenger sale is the collector's way to move properties that carry long-running delinquent tax, and section 21-260 sets its rules. Unsold parcels are offered again each year.

  • The minimum bid is $250, or one-half of the tax if the total liability is under $500.
  • A sale is not final until the court confirms it.
  • On confirmation it extinguishes the in rem lien of the general taxes, but the owner's personal liability for the tax remains.
  • The certificate holder may petition for a tax deed within 6 months before the redemption period ends.
  • Redemption after a sale on or after September 9, 1993 carries interest of 3% per month for the first 2 months, then 12%, 24%, 36% and 48% across the later periods, and 6% per year after 24 months.

Except for owner-occupied single-family units, a redemption from a scavenger sale also requires payment of other taxes that were delinquent when the sale occurred.

How should a seller with a tax-sale parcel proceed?

Start by learning where the parcel sits on the timeline, since the answer drives every option.

  • Ask the county collector whether the taxes were sold, and ask the county clerk for the sale date, certificate number and redemption deadline.
  • Request the redemption total in writing and keep the receipt for any deposit.
  • Read each court notice and calendar the hearing date.
  • Tell any title company about the certificate before you sign a contract, because a recorded tax deed is a separate event from a sale you make.
  • Remember that tax deeds are exempt from the state transfer tax under section 31-45, while a voluntary sale by the owner is not.

A buyer who purchases as is and pays cash can close faster than a financed buyer, which matters when the redemption date is close. The redemption itself still has to be made to the county clerk by the deadline.

More questions about Illinois Tax Sales

How long is the redemption period after an Illinois tax sale?

For certificates issued on or after January 1, 2024, the general period is 3 years from the date of sale under 35 ILCS 200/21-350, with exceptions that begin with vacant property. Ask the county clerk for the deadline on your certificate.

Can I lose my house at an Illinois tax sale?

The sale itself does not move title. The tax buyer must give notices, file a petition and win a court order for a tax deed or judicial tax deed auction after the redemption period passes.

Who receives the redemption payment?

The county clerk. Section 21-355 requires the deposit to be payable to the county clerk and received before the close of business on the last day, or postmarked at least one day earlier.

What is the highest penalty a bidder can offer at an Illinois tax sale?

A bid cannot exceed a 9% penalty on the tax or special assessment, and the bidder offering the lowest penalty percentage wins under section 21-215.

Is a tax deed subject to the Illinois transfer tax?

No. Tax deeds are exempt from the state transfer tax under 35 ILCS 200/31-45, although a voluntary sale by an owner is taxed at the state rate.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Illinois foreclosures go through court, and owners have a statutory redemption period.

What the official sources say

  • Redemption period for residential real estate ends on the later of (i) 7 months from the date all mortgagors were served/submitted to jurisdiction or (ii) 3 months from entry of judgment of foreclosure; for non-residential foreclosures it is the later of 6 months from service or 3 months from judgment. (735 ILCS 5/15-1603(b)(1)-(2) (as amended P.A. 104-417, eff. 8-15-25); source)
  • Redemption period is shortened to the later of the end of any reinstatement period or 60 days after judgment if the court finds the value is under 90% of the redemption amount and the mortgagee waives deficiency; shortened to 30 days after judgment if the property is abandoned. (735 ILCS 5/15-1603(b)(3)-(4); source)
  • Owner of redemption must give written notice of intent to redeem to mortgagee's attorney at least 15 days (excluding weekends/court holidays) before the designated redemption date; once expired, the right of redemption is not revived. (735 ILCS 5/15-1603(e), (c)(1); source)
  • Circuit Court of Cook County Chancery Division runs a Mortgage Foreclosure Mediation Program: homeowners who received a court summons get free housing counseling and legal assistance; first step is a free meeting with a housing counselor via toll-free helpline (855) 452-2637; homeowners not yet in foreclosure are referred to Cook County Legal Aid for Housing and Debt (855) 956-5763. (Circuit Court of Cook County, Chancery Division Mediation page (no statute cited); source)

What we could not confirm

  • Illinois deficiency rules were not confirmed.

Illinois foreclosure FAQ

Can I sell my house during foreclosure?

Yes. A cash sale can pay the lender from the proceeds if it closes in time. Ask for a payoff figure.

How does foreclosure work in Illinois?

Illinois uses judicial foreclosure under Article XV of the Code of Civil Procedure, known as the Illinois Mortgage Foreclosure Law. A lender files a lawsuit, the homeowner is served, the court enters a judgment of foreclosure, a redemption period runs, and a court-supervised sale follows. The court must then confirm the sale before a deed passes. Every stage gives the owner a decision point, which is why the timeline matters to anyone thinking about selling.

The law contains several protections that owners often miss. A homeowner may reinstate the mortgage, redeem after judgment, object to the court's jurisdiction, or work out a deed in lieu or a consent foreclosure. Selling the house before the judicial sale is another route, because the sale proceeds can pay off the mortgage. The main stages are:

  • Complaint filed and the owner served with summons.
  • Reinstatement window of 90 days from service.
  • Judgment of foreclosure.
  • Redemption period, usually the later of two measures described below.
  • Judicial sale, then court confirmation and a deed.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Illinois house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Can an Illinois owner reinstate the mortgage?

Yes, for a limited time. Section 15-1602 lets a mortgagor reinstate by curing all existing defaults, apart from the part of the principal that would not have been due without acceleration, and by paying the costs and expenses the mortgage requires for those defaults. The cure has to happen before 90 days have passed from the date every mortgagor was served with summons or by publication, or otherwise submitted to the court's jurisdiction. For service by publication, the first date of publication starts the count.

On reinstatement the foreclosure is dismissed and the mortgage documents continue as if there had been no acceleration. The right is not used up by one exercise, but where the court makes an express written finding that the owner reinstated, the same relief is unavailable under that mortgage for five years from the dismissal. The court may enter a judgment before the 90 days expire, subject to the owner's continuing right to reinstate.

How long is the redemption period after a foreclosure judgment?

For a mortgage on residential real estate, section 15-1603 ends redemption on the later of two dates: 7 months from the date all mortgagors were served or submitted to the court, or 3 months from entry of the judgment of foreclosure. For other property the first measure is 6 months. The statute was amended by Public Act 104-417, effective August 15, 2025.

Redemption period rules in 735 ILCS 5/15-1603(b)
SituationRedemption period ends
Residential real estate when the case beganLater of 7 months after service or 3 months after judgment
All other foreclosuresLater of 6 months after service or 3 months after judgment
Value under 90% of the redemption amount, and lender waives deficiencyLater of the end of any reinstatement period or 60 days after judgment
Court finds the property abandoned30 days after judgment

Once the period expires it is never revived. It runs on its own clock, and the filing of another case or a stay of the sale does not toll it. A court that does stay the period extends it by the days left or by 30 days after the stay ends, whichever is later.

What does it take to redeem the property?

Only an owner of redemption can redeem, and only during the period and if the right was not validly waived. The amount is the judgment figure, which covers principal and accrued interest due on the judgment date, costs the law allows, court-approved expenses and attorney fees where the mortgage provides for them, sums advanced under section 15-1505, and per diem interest from judgment to redemption at the mortgage rate as if no default had occurred. Expenses the lender reasonably incurs after judgment are added once certified.

The owner must give written notice of intent to redeem to the lender's attorney of record, naming the redemption date and a current address, and file a certification of that notice with the clerk. The attorney must receive it at least 15 days before the date, not counting Saturdays, Sundays or court holidays. The lender then has to file a certification of expenses and give notice at least 3 such days before the date. If the lender refuses payment or the owner objects to the extra expenses, the owner pays the certified amount to the clerk with a written statement of the objection, and the court holds a hearing on the disputed funds.

When redemption is paid, the lender must promptly provide a release of the mortgage or a satisfaction of the judgment. If nobody redeems, the property is sold.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Illinois houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How is an Illinois foreclosure sale held and confirmed?

After the reinstatement and redemption periods expire, section 15-1507 calls for a sale on the terms set in the judgment, conducted by a judge, sheriff or other designated person. The lender may ask that the sale take place in person, online, or both. Public notice runs in a newspaper for 3 consecutive calendar weeks, with the first notice no more than 45 days before the sale and the last at least 7 days before it. Parties who have appeared also receive notice within that same 45 to 7 day span.

The buyer gets a receipt, and once the bid is paid in full a recordable certificate of sale that remains subject to court confirmation. Under 15-1508, the court enters an order confirming the sale. In residential cases the owner receives a mailed notice with boldface language about the right to remain in possession for 30 days after an order of possession. If the sale price falls short of the debt, the order may include a personal judgment for a deficiency where it was requested and the borrower was personally served or appeared. After confirmation and payment, the court executes a deed under 15-1509.

Who can stay in the house during an Illinois foreclosure?

Before judgment, section 15-1701 says the owner of residential real estate is entitled to possession unless the lender objects, shows good cause, is authorized by the mortgage, and persuades the court that it will probably win. From the judgment through the 30th day after the sale is confirmed, the owner may be required to pay monthly the lesser of the contract interest or the fair rental value to stay between the end of redemption and that 30th day.

After 30 days from the confirmation order, the purchaser is entitled to possession against the parties whose interests were terminated. For tenants the rules are gentler. A bona fide lease of a dwelling unit cannot be ended by the new owner except through Article IX, and leases are not terminated automatically when a lender takes possession. A supplemental eviction petition against an occupant not named in the case may be filed up to 90 days after the confirmation order, with a hearing no sooner than 21 days after service, and a current-on-rent tenant may keep possession for up to 120 days or the lease term, whichever is shorter.

What choices does an owner have besides waiting for a sale?

Several, and some are faster than a full case.

  • Deed in lieu. Under 15-1401, a lender may accept a deed in lieu of foreclosure, which relieves everyone who owes the secured debt, including guarantors, of personal liability unless they agree otherwise in a contemporaneous document. Merely tendering or recording a deed does not count as acceptance.
  • Consent foreclosure. Section 15-1402 lets the court vest title in the lender when it waives any deficiency and every mortgagor consents, and the judgment bars a deficiency claim.
  • Jurisdiction objection. In residential cases a motion to dismiss or quash service on personal jurisdiction is due 60 days after the owner files an appearance or takes part in a hearing, unless the court extends the time (15-1505.6). Filing another pleading first waives the objection.
  • Sell the house. A buyer who closes before the judicial sale can pay the lender from proceeds. Ask the lender for a written payoff figure and give the title company the case number.
You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Is there free help for Cook County homeowners in foreclosure?

The Circuit Court of Cook County runs a Mortgage Foreclosure Mediation Program through its Chancery Division. Homeowners who have received a court summons can get housing counseling and legal assistance at no charge, and the first step is a free meeting with a housing counselor arranged through the program's toll-free helpline at (855) 452-2637. Homeowners who worry about their mortgage but have no summons are directed to Cook County Legal Aid for Housing and Debt at (855) 956-5763. Details are on the Chancery Division mediation page. Outside Cook County, ask the circuit clerk whether the local court offers a similar program.

More questions about Illinois Foreclosure Process

How long does an Illinois homeowner have to reinstate a mortgage?

Until 90 days after every mortgagor was served with summons, or otherwise submitted to the court. For service by publication, the first publication date starts the count. The owner cures the defaults and pays the required costs and expenses, and the case is then dismissed.

Does an Illinois owner keep the right to redeem after the sale?

No. The redemption period ends before the judicial sale, and once it expires the right is not revived. The owner has to pay the judgment amount and give written notice of intent to redeem at least 15 days ahead, not counting weekends and court holidays, so planning has to start well before the end date.

Can a lender collect a deficiency after a foreclosure sale in Illinois?

It can in some cases. The order confirming the sale may include a personal judgment for the shortfall when the complaint asked for it, the proof supports it, and the borrower was personally served or appeared. A consent foreclosure bars it, and so does the 60 day shortened redemption route that depends on a waiver.

What happens to a tenant when an Illinois house is foreclosed?

A bona fide lease of a dwelling unit survives the sale and can be ended only through Article IX, with at least 90 days of written notice. A tenant who is current on rent may keep possession for up to 120 days after notice of a supplemental eviction hearing, or for the lease term if shorter.

Can I sell my house while the foreclosure case is open?

Yes. A sale that closes before the court-supervised sale can pay the lender from the proceeds. Ask the lender for a payoff statement, tell the title company about the case, and have an attorney confirm what must be filed to end the lawsuit.

What the official sources say

  • Landlord may demand rent and notify tenant in writing that unless paid within a stated time, not less than 5 days after service, the lease will be terminated; if unpaid, landlord may commence eviction without further notice. Notice must prominently state the partial-payment language specified in the statute. (735 ILCS 5/9-209; source)

Applies only to the pilot district, not all of Chicago. (Chicago Municipal Code ch. 5-11 (5-11-050, 5-11-060); source)

What we could not confirm

  • Chicago RLTO sale provisions were not opened.

How does an eviction case move through an Illinois court?

An Illinois eviction is a court case under Article IX of the Code of Civil Procedure, and only a judge can order a tenant out. The sequence runs from a written demand or notice, to a complaint and summons, to a trial, to an eviction order that the sheriff enforces. Each step has its own statute, and skipping one gives the tenant an argument to delay or dismiss the case.

For a landlord thinking about selling, the timeline matters more than any single rule. A buyer who wants the house empty at closing has to wait for the whole sequence, and a seller who has not started it yet is looking at weeks or months of uncertainty. The court steps are:

  • Notice or demand served on the tenant.
  • Complaint filed in the circuit court of the county where the property sits, and a summons issued by the clerk.
  • Trial, with or without the tenant present.
  • Eviction order and, if the court allows, a stay.
  • Enforcement by the sheriff within the life of the order.

Who can bring an eviction case, and on what grounds?

The person entitled to possession can ask the court to restore it. Section 9-102 lists the circumstances, including a forcible entry, entry into vacant property without right or title, and a lessee who holds on after the lease ends by its own terms or by notice to quit. It also reaches a buyer under a purchase agreement who failed to perform and a former owner who will not leave after a court sale or a mortgage sale once any redemption period has run.

Condominium and common interest community boards have their own track. They may sue when an owner fails to pay a share of common expenses after the board serves the statutory demand and the time stated in it runs out. A tenant of such an owner can also be removed if the lease breaks the association rules and the board follows the demand procedure.

What does the complaint and summons stage involve?

Under 9-106, the party entitled to possession files a complaint in the circuit court for the county where the property is, describes the premises with reasonable certainty, and says the named defendant unlawfully withholds it. The clerk then issues a summons. A complaint may not name a minor as a defendant, and one that does is dismissed in full against every defendant and sealed.

The tenant may raise any defense under a general denial, but the statute keeps the case narrow: matters not germane to the purpose of the proceeding cannot come in by counterclaim, with the exception of the section on premises used for crime. A claim for rent may be joined in the same complaint, and the judgment can include the amount found due.

When personal service fails, the plaintiff can file an affidavit that the defendant cannot be found, and the court allows notice by posting and mailing or by publication and mailing (9-107). The sheriff posts three copies in three public places near the courthouse at least 10 days before the appearance date. In that case the court may rule only on possession, not on a joined rent claim, if the tenant never appears.

What happens at trial and after judgment?

If the defendant was properly summoned and does not appear, the trial may go ahead without them and without a jury (9-109). Where both sides appear, the plaintiff must prove the complaint by a preponderance of the evidence, and then the court enters an eviction order (9-109.5).

An order does not last forever. Section 9-117 speaks of a plaintiff having 120 days after judgment for the sheriff to carry it out, and it lets a plaintiff ask the court to extend the order after that window with a notice to the tenant. The court grants the extension unless the tenant shows that the tenancy was reinstated, the breach was cured or waived, the parties made a post-judgment agreement the tenant has kept, or other legal or equitable grounds bar enforcement.

After a landlord wins, the landlord must still try to limit losses. Section 9-213.1 requires reasonable measures to mitigate damages against a defaulting lessee, and 9-203 sets double rent for a tenant who gives notice to leave on a date and then stays.

What should an owner do about a tenant before selling a rented house?

Start by finding out which clock is running. A tenant on a valid fixed lease with rent current is in a very different position from one who already received a notice. Gather the lease, the rent ledger, the notices with proof of service, and any court papers, then give them to the attorney and the title company before signing a listing or purchase agreement.

  • If the lease is in force and the tenant pays, a buyer who wants an investment property may take the house with the tenant in place.
  • If the tenant is behind, decide whether to serve the rent demand and file, or to negotiate a written move-out date, possibly with relocation money.
  • If a judgment already exists, ask the circuit clerk how many days remain on the order and whether an extension is needed.
  • If the house is in foreclosure, the bona fide lease rules in the foreclosure statute apply and may protect the tenant for 90 days after the new owner takes control.

A cash buyer that buys as-is can sometimes close with the tenant still inside and handle the occupancy afterward. That choice should be written into the contract so there is no confusion about who bears the court costs.

Where can landlords and tenants find help with an Illinois eviction?

The Illinois Courts website keeps approved statewide eviction forms that all circuit courts must accept. It also points to guided interviews from Illinois Legal Aid Online for a landlord filing a complaint, a tenant answering one, and a person asking to remove an eviction file from public view. Rental assistance through the statewide court-based program requires a pending eviction case. Read the Illinois Courts eviction page and call the circuit clerk in the county where the house is for local filing practice.

More questions about Illinois Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Can an Illinois landlord change the locks to force a tenant out?

The statute lays out a path of complaint, summons, trial and an order that the sheriff enforces, and nothing in Article IX describes a lockout. Ask an attorney before taking any step outside that path.

How long does a landlord have to carry out an Illinois eviction order?

The statute refers to a 120 day window after judgment. If the sheriff does not act within it, the plaintiff can ask the court to extend the order after giving the tenant a notice of hearing. The court grants the request unless the tenant shows a listed ground, such as cure of the breach or a kept post-judgment agreement.

Can a tenant stay after a default judgment?

The case can go forward without the tenant. If the tenant was properly summoned and did not appear, the court may try the case without them and enter an eviction order. A tenant who wants to contest the case can get response forms through the Illinois Courts site.

What is the standard of proof in an Illinois eviction trial?

A preponderance of the evidence. Section 9-109.5 says that when the court finds the complaint's allegations proven by that standard, it enters an eviction order for the plaintiff. Anyone building a case should bring the lease, the notice, proof of service and the rent records.

Does a landlord have to try to re-rent a unit after a tenant defaults?

Yes. Section 9-213.1 requires a landlord or agent to take reasonable measures to mitigate the damages recoverable against a defaulting lessee. Keep a record of showings and advertising so the court can see what steps were taken.
